subject: Communication
title: Can You Really Spot a Liar?
description: A micro-lesson that makes Can You Really Spot a Liar? usable.

hook.text: People think they can spot liars. Research says we're right about 54% of the time — barely better than a coin flip.

buildup.text: Police, judges, and psychologists all perform at roughly chance level when detecting deception in studies.

discovery.text: We look for the wrong cues: fidgeting, gaze aversion, and nervousness — which also appear in truthful anxious people.

twist.text: Liars don't always squirm. Skilled liars are often calmer than truth-tellers because they've rehearsed.

climax.text: No single cue reliably detects deception. The best approach looks for inconsistencies across multiple channels.

punchline.text: There's no Pinocchio's nose. Lie detection is hard for everyone.

quiz.question: How accurate are most people at detecting lies?

details.summary: Despite popular belief, humans are barely better than chance at detecting lies—averaging about 54% accuracy. No single body language cue reliably indicates deception, and confidence in lie detection often exceeds ability.
details.whyItMatters: Overconfidence in lie detection leads to false accusations, wrongful convictions, and broken trust, making humility about this skill essential.
takeaways: Average lie detection accuracy is only slightly above chance
No single nonverbal cue reliably indicates deception
Confidence in lie detection is unrelated to actual accuracy

faq.question: Why are humans so bad at detecting lies?
faq.answer: We rely on stereotypical cues like gaze aversion and fidgeting that liars learn to suppress. We also have a truth bias—a default assumption that others are honest. Practiced liars exploit both tendencies effectively.

faq.question: Are some people naturally better at spotting lies?
faq.answer: A small number of people (called 'wizards' by Paul Ekman) consistently outperform others, but they are extremely rare. Most professionals, including police and judges, perform no better than untrained individuals.
